title: What to Know About Shark Season: Risks, Attacks and More

contentUnits.title: Fear is bigger than the baseline risk
contentUnits.text: The source story opens by separating shark fear from shark probability: attacks are rare, but risk is not zero. The VR version starts underwater with the source shark nearby, then pulls the viewer back to the larger context.

contentUnits.title: Where and when matters most
contentUnits.text: The original interactive asks readers to choose a coast. This beat turns the coast into a ring of risk stations, showing how region and season change the odds.

contentUnits.title: Florida counts bites; Hawaii and California carry severity
contentUnits.text: The adaptation groups the source regional notes into a concise comparison: Florida is the frequency center, Hawaii has serious tiger-shark encounters, and California/New England are white-shark severity stories.

contentUnits.title: The story is about a few species, not all sharks
contentUnits.text: Rather than surrounding the reader with danger, this beat compares roles: bull and tiger sharks explain many serious warnings, blacktips explain many minor bites, and nurse sharks carry the do-not-harass lesson.

contentUnits.title: What you do in the water changes the risk
contentUnits.text: The original article shifts from place to behavior. The VR beat stages board sports, swimming, fishing, and shark handling as separate exposure stations so the reader sees risk as a set of choices.

contentUnits.title: Make yourself clearly not shark food
contentUnits.text: The practical guidance becomes a calm checklist in space: group up, avoid low light, stay away from prey activity, skip shiny contrast, and do not bother sharks.

contentUnits.title: Fight hard, get out, control bleeding
contentUnits.text: The source story treats an attack as unlikely but actionable. If a shark holds on, strike vulnerable areas, leave the water without panic, and use bleeding-control preparation.

contentUnits.title: The risk is extremely small, but preparation is real
contentUnits.text: The closing beat preserves the article position: knowing the numbers may not erase fear, but clear behavior makes the already-small risk smaller.

regions.label: California
regions.note: Few bites, but large white sharks make serious outcomes more likely.

regions.label: Carolinas + GA
regions.note: Warm months bring sharks and swimmers into the same water.

regions.label: Florida
regions.note: Highest U.S. bite count; Volusia County is a major hotspot.

regions.label: Gulf Coast
regions.note: Lower incident count; murky water and fishing can raise local risk.

regions.label: Hawaii
regions.note: Fewer bites than Florida but a higher share of serious attacks.

regions.label: Mid-Atlantic
regions.note: Popular beaches, but relatively few recorded attacks.

regions.label: New England
regions.note: Seal populations can bring white sharks close to shore.

regions.label: PNW + Alaska
regions.note: Very few recorded incidents despite long coastlines.
